title: Deep-Sea Microbes Get a Pressure-Cooked Meal from Marine Snow
summary:
In the sunless abyss, a newly discovered food source sustains deep-sea microbes: marine snow particles, squeezed by immense pressure, leak dissolved carbon and nitrogen. A University of Southern Denmark study published in Science Advances reveals that this leakage provides an immediate, crucial energy supply for microbes in nutrient-starved depths.

Marine snow — clumps of dead algae, microbes, and organic debris — drifts downward. At 2 to 6 kilometers deep, hydrostatic pressure becomes so intense it forces out dissolved organic matter. “The pressure acts almost like a giant juicer,” says lead author Peter Stief. “It squeezes dissolved organic compounds out of the particles, and microbes can use them immediately.”

Using laboratory-created marine snow from diatoms in rotating pressure tanks, researchers measured leakage. Up to half of a particle’s carbon escaped, mostly as proteins and carbohydrates. Within 48 hours, bacterial abundance increased 30-fold, and respiration soared. The same pattern occurred across multiple diatom species, suggesting a widespread ocean phenomenon.

This challenges the long-held view that most marine snow carbon becomes buried in sediments. Instead, much remains suspended in deep water for centuries, potentially returning to the atmosphere. “This process affects how much carbon the ocean can store and for how long,” Stief notes, with implications for climate models. Future research will move from lab to open ocean.
why_it_matters: This microscopic meal chain affects the whole planet’s climate by controlling how much carbon dioxide the ocean can trap. If pressure-squeezed carbon stays in the water instead of settling on the seafloor, it may re-enter the air sooner, influencing global temperatures that today’s teens will inherit.

background_read: The deep ocean, often called the abyss, is cold, dark, and extremely nutrient-poor. Unlike sunlit surface waters, where tiny plants called phytoplankton bloom, life on the seafloor depends mostly on a slow, steady rain of organic particles — marine snow. Scientists have long known that this snow carries carbon from the surface to the depths, but what happens to that carbon under immense pressure was less clear.

Hydrostatic pressure increases by one atmosphere for every 10 meters of water depth. At 4 kilometers, pressures are over 400 times sea-level pressure, enough to crush most submarines. The research team from the University of Southern Denmark created artificial marine snow from diatoms (common algae) and placed it in high-pressure tanks that simulated the deep sea. They found that the pressure acts like a juicer, forcing out dissolved organic compounds that hungry bacteria can immediately use.

This discovery, published in Science Advances (a respected open-access journal) and led by Peter Stief, shifts the understanding of how carbon moves through the ocean. Instead of most of it being locked away in seafloor sediments for millions of years, a significant fraction may stay suspended in the water column, potentially re-entering the atmosphere over centuries.

perspectives.description: The discovery fills a gap in the ocean’s carbon cycle, helping scientists build more accurate climate models. Knowing that pressure-released carbon feeds deep-sea bacteria can lead to better predictions of how much CO₂ the ocean will absorb in a warming world.

If more carbon stays dissolved in deep waters rather than being locked in sediments, the ocean’s ability to act as a long-term carbon sink may be weaker than previously believed. This could mean that human-caused CO₂ has a bigger, faster impact on atmospheric warming.

The work reveals a previously unknown physical squeeze on marine snow, complementing biological decay. It shows that chemical and physical forces work together to make deep-sea ecosystems function, and that lab experiments can simulate abyssal conditions in ways field studies cannot.

Future open-ocean experiments will test whether the same leakage occurs in real deep waters and with different types of plankton. If confirmed, global ocean models will have to be updated, possibly changing how nations plan carbon emissions targets.
